questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Set out how a follow-up process should treat a finding that stays open
questions.stem: An audit finding on the maintenance of point heating has been open for two years without closure. Explain in one paragraph how a follow-up process should treat a finding that keeps recurring.

answer.exemplar: A finding that recurs should be treated as evidence about the system rather than about the individuals who happened to hold the post at the time. The first step is to restate it in terms of the control that failed, so that it can be tested rather than merely discussed, and to name a single owner who can deliver it. The second step is to require evidence of operation rather than a statement of intention, because a manager's assurance that a new procedure exists is not the same as a sample of records showing it was used. Third, an aging threshold should be defined in advance, above which the finding is reported publicly with the reasons it remains open, so that repetition carries a cost. Closure should then require either a verified control or a recorded acceptance of the risk by a named senior officer, with the risk accepted recorded rather than implied by silence.

questions.explanation: A strong answer requires the finding to be restated as a control failure, tested by evidence of operation rather than assurance, and reported publicly once it ages, with closure only on verification or recorded risk acceptance.
questions.hint: Ask what evidence would close it.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the scope of an audit mandate shapes what it can find
questions.stem: Explain, for a board, why the scope of an audit office's mandate determines what it can find.

answer.exemplar: A mandate is a statement of what the office is entitled to look at, and it bounds the evidence available to it. If an audit office is asked only to check that payments match approved sums, it can detect an unauthorised payment but cannot say whether a diesel generator was ever installed, because the physical asset lies outside its scope. If the mandate reaches the records behind the transaction, the same office can trace a depot's fuel reconciliation to the log entries behind it and say where the record and the fuel disagree. Extending the mandate therefore changes what counts as a finding, not merely how many pages a report contains. Boards that want a particular kind of assurance must set the scope to match, and must give the office the powers of access and the cooperation from operators that the scope assumes.

questions.explanation: A strong answer explains that the mandate bounds the evidence available, so a narrow scope produces findings about sums only, and that matching the mandate to the assurance required is what makes deeper findings possible.
questions.hint: Ask what the office may examine.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a declaration must record both assets and liabilities
questions.stem: A declaration form records a house, a vehicle, cash and shares, and separately records a mortgage and a car loan. Explain why both sets of figures belong on the form.

answer.exemplar: Net worth is the value of what a person owns less what they owe, so a declaration that lists only assets reports a gross figure that can be very misleading. A house bought with a mortgage at 95 per cent of its value appears as a large asset while the corresponding liability, which is most of the purchase, is omitted, so the declared position overstates the stake in the property by the whole mortgage. Because the point of the declaration is to show what interests a person holds in public office, the measure that matters is the equity at stake, not the gross value of the property. The same applies to a vehicle bought on credit and to shares held against a loan. Recording liabilities also prevents a declarant from presenting borrowed wealth as their own, and it allows the figures to be checked, since a mortgage is registered and a loan appears in the lender's records, so the two sides can be reconciled against external evidence rather than accepted on trust.

questions.explanation: A strong answer explains that net worth is assets less liabilities, that a mortgage omitted while the house is listed overstates the interest held, and that registering the debt makes the figures checkable against outside records.
questions.hint: Ask what the declaration is meant to measure.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why off-budget funds weaken budgetary control
questions.stem: A depot runs a fund for staff meals, a fund for crew recreation and a fund for training bursaries, none of which appears in the published budget. Explain, for a board, why this arrangement weakens budget control.

answer.exemplar: Control over money depends on three things being joined together: the authority to spend, the appropriation that permits the spending, and the report that shows what was spent. An off-budget fund breaks the link between the second and the third. The appropriation is set at a level for the whole department, and the fund is then spent from outside it, so the department's authority to spend exceeds the sum the legislature approved and no single published figure reveals by how much. The consequence is that the budget ceases to be a reliable statement of what will be spent, which affects every other use of the budget, from scrutiny to the allocation of the next year's sums. Where the funds are small, the argument is often made that including them would clutter the budget, but that argument misreads what the budget is for: it is a statement of the organisation's total commitments, and a small fund that is excluded is still a commitment. Consolidation into named lines costs little and restores the link between authority, appropriation and report for each of them.

questions.explanation: A strong answer explains that control requires authority, appropriation and reporting to be joined, that excluding funds makes the budget an unreliable statement of commitments, and that consolidation restores the link at little cost.
questions.hint: Ask what the budget promises about spending.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Choose how to handle a recurring audit finding
questions.stem: An audit finding on overtime authorisation stays open for three years and is raised in each annual report. Which approach best handles a finding that keeps recurring?

options.text: Restate the finding with a named owner and a deadline, and report it publicly until closed
Close the finding and rely on management to apply the recommendation
options.misconception: removes the pressure without checking whether anything changed

options.text: Reclassify the finding as a management matter outside the audit plan
options.misconception: relabels the problem rather than resolving it

options.text: Reduce the finding's priority so that it no longer counts towards the audit score
options.misconception: hides the recurring issue from published results

questions.explanation: A recurring finding indicates that the underlying control has not changed, so restating it with a named owner, a deadline and public reporting makes progress visible and creates cost for non-delivery. Closing, relabelling or deprioritising all remove the pressure without changing the control.
questions.hint: Ask what makes delay costly.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Count the reports that satisfy a protection rule
questions.stem: Of 120 safety reports, 95 were made in writing within seven days, 12 were written but late, 9 were oral, and 4 were anonymous. How many reports meet a protection rule requiring a written report within seven days?

options.text: 95 reports, because those are the ones both written and lodged in time
107 reports, which includes the written reports that arrived late
options.misconception: includes reports that fail the stated deadline

options.text: 116 reports, which adds the oral reports to those made in writing
options.misconception: counts reports that fail the written condition

options.text: 120 reports, because every report in the file reached the inspector
options.misconception: treats receipt as satisfying the conditions

questions.explanation: Only the 95 reports both written and lodged in time meet the conditions; oral, late and anonymous reports each fail one. The distractors include the late reports, add the oral ones, or treat receipt as enough.
questions.hint: Count only the reports meeting both conditions.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why concentrated reporting needs careful interpretation
questions.stem: Explain, for a board, why reports of safety concerns from a small number of staff need careful interpretation.

answer.exemplar: A concentration of reports looks alarming and is usually less alarming than it appears, because reporting tracks exposure to conditions rather than care or honesty. Staff notice what they encounter daily, so a small group working a particular route, shift or depot will encounter the same defect every time and report it repeatedly. Treating their output as evidence that they are unusually conscientious would also penalise them relative to colleagues who say nothing, which discourages future reporting. The pattern should instead be read as a prompt to investigate the conditions behind it, which is often the most productive use of the data: the repeated reports identify a persistent hazard that single isolated reports would have missed. Two errors should be avoided in reaching that conclusion, which is that silence elsewhere may mean acceptance rather than absence of risk, and that even a well-founded explanation for the pattern is not an explanation for every individual report within it.

questions.explanation: A strong answer explains that reporting reflects exposure to conditions rather than diligence, that the pattern should prompt investigation of the hazard behind it, and that it also carries risks of ignoring other staff and of excusing every report.
questions.hint: Ask what staff encounter, not who they are.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the uncommitted balance of an off-budget maintenance fund
questions.stem: A signalling maintenance fund of 480,000 pounds is held outside the published transport budget. Of that, 35 per cent was spent on urgent signal repairs and 20 per cent on depot ventilation. How many pounds remained for other maintenance work?

questions.hint: Find the percentage left before applying it.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the feature of a declaration form that distorts published wealth

stimulus.body: Section 2 asks the declarant to list the value of property, vehicles, investments and cash. Section 3 asks for loans and mortgages to be declared, but states that any secured debt on the declared property may instead be noted in the free-text box. Section 4 provides that declarations are published in full unless the declarant requests otherwise, in which case the values are published but the descriptions are withheld.

questions.stem: According to the form, which feature most risks distorting the published picture of declared wealth?

options.text: The form asks only for values, without describing the assets
options.misconception: treats brevity of description as the distortion risk

options.text: Debt may be left out of the declaration if it is noted in a free-text box
Declarations are published in full unless the declarant requests otherwise
options.misconception: reads an opt-out as creating a reporting duty

options.text: The form requires property, vehicles, investments and cash to be listed
options.misconception: mistakes comprehensiveness of assets for a weakness

questions.explanation: Letting secured debt be moved into a free-text box lets the headline declaration omit the liabilities that net worth depends on, so published figures are no longer comparable. Brevity of description, an opt-out from publishing and a comprehensive asset list are not distortions of the measure.
questions.hint: Look for where liabilities can be set aside.

questions.stem: An audit office reviews spending, compliance and the reliability of operational records. Which arrangement best protects the credibility of its work?

options.misconception: makes the auditor dependent on operational cooperation

options.text: Let the office publish only conclusions, keeping the working papers closed
options.misconception: removes the evidence that supports the conclusions

options.text: Let the office set the operational targets it then audits
options.misconception: lets the audited party define the standard

options.text: Let the office set its own work programme and publish its method and findings

options.text: Note the recommendation as implemented in the next annual report
options.misconception: treats a report entry as evidence of operation

options.text: Re-date the finding to the next audit cycle and carry it forward
options.misconception: defers rather than verifies

options.misconception: assumes capacity alone secures independence

options.misconception: infers capture from one quarter of findings

options.misconception: infers control from plurality alone

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose and the weaknesses of a confidential reporting route
questions.stem: Explain, for a board, what a confidential reporting route is for, and what its weaknesses are.

answer.exemplar: A confidential reporting route exists because the ordinary channels fail in exactly the situations where reporting matters most. Staff who witness wrongdoing in a small depot, or who fear the consequences of complaining about their own supervisor, will not use a route that identifies them to the person they are reporting. A confidential route lowers that cost by separating the reporter's identity from the substance of the report and by protecting the reporter when a disclosure proves well founded. Its weaknesses are the mirror image of its strengths. If reports are anonymous, they cannot be clarified, and an incomplete account may be investigated at great cost and dismissed on a technicality. If identity is kept confidential, the body cannot assure the reporter that the organisation has not identified them, and confidence erodes. Protection is therefore usually conditional rather than absolute, and the condition must be enforceable, with a clear test, a deadline and a named decision-maker, otherwise the route becomes an easy way to refuse protection.

questions.explanation: A strong answer explains that the route exists to overcome the failure of ordinary channels where reprisal is feared, and that conditional protection is the only workable compromise because anonymity blocks clarification.
questions.hint: Ask what the route has to trade away.

questions.learningObjective: Classify balances by their relationship to the published budget

stimulus.body: Balances at 31 March: signal renewal reserve 2,400,000 pounds; crew welfare fund 61,000 pounds; depot canteen account 18,500 pounds; rolling stock warranty claim 3,100,000 pounds. questions.stem: According to the note, which balance is best treated as an off-budget account?

options.text: The crew welfare fund, which is held outside the budget and spent by managers
The signal renewal reserve, because it is large and ring-fenced
options.misconception: confuses a large ring-fenced reserve with an off-budget account

options.text: The warranty claim, because it arose outside the normal budget process
options.misconception: mistakes a receivable from a settlement for an account

options.text: The depot canteen account, because small accounts are always outside the budget
options.misconception: assumes size determines the budget treatment

questions.explanation: The welfare fund is money the authority holds and spends outside the published budget, which is what makes it off-budget. A ring-fenced reserve stays within the budget, and a settlement receivable is an asset owed to the authority rather than a fund to spend.
questions.hint: Ask whether the money is spent outside the budget.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Reporting lines of an integrity body
questions.learningObjective: Explain why reporting lines matter more than headcount for an integrity body
questions.stem: Explain, for a board, why the reporting lines of an integrity body matter more than its headcount.

answer.exemplar: Headcount determines how much work a body can do, but reporting lines determine whether that work can be used against the organisation it examines. If investigators report to the managing director of the network, every case involves a conversation with the person whose conduct may be in question, and the pressure to handle it internally grows with every case. If the same investigators report to a board committee that appoints them, sets their budget and receives their findings, then the flow of information runs away from the operational chain rather than through it. The headcount question is real but is answered by resourcing, whereas the reporting question decides whether the body can survive the first serious finding it makes. Boards that add investigators without changing the reporting line usually find a body that is busy, well informed and unable to publish anything that its own organisation would object to.

questions.explanation: A strong answer contrasts capacity with usability, explaining that reporting lines determine whether findings can survive contact with the organisation, and that more staff on the same line simply produce more unusable work.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the first serious finding.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The accountability problem of an integrity body
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a well-staffed integrity body can still fail to hold an organisation to account
questions.stem: Explain, for a board, why an integrity body can fail to hold the organisation accountable even when it is well staffed.

answer.exemplar: Capacity and accountability are separate. A well-staffed body can still fail if its mandate is narrow, if its findings are filtered before they leave the organisation, or if nobody is obliged to act on them. A mandate that excludes the decisions of the board itself leaves the most senior level untouched. Filtering, in the form of legal review of every draft report, converts the body's output into a negotiated product and makes it hard for an outsider to tell whose view it is. And even a public finding changes nothing unless a named person must respond and a forum requires the response to be published. Boards should therefore test three things: the reach of the mandate, whether findings reach the public unedited, and whether a response is required from a named officer. Staffing without those three simply produces a busy body with nothing to show.

questions.explanation: A strong answer shows that capacity is not the constraint, and identifies mandate reach, filtering of findings and the absence of any required response as the three failures that leave a body unable to hold the organisation to account.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a finding once it is issued.

questions.learningObjective: Explain a fall in claims while the underlying service measure holds steady

stimulus.body: Drivers may claim 40 pence for each journey that departs no more than two minutes late and is completed without a passenger complaint. The note states that claims must be lodged by the driver within 48 hours of the shift ending, and that only journeys covered by a working timetable qualify. Following a change to the claim form, claims fell from 310 to 190 per month, while the punctuality rate was unchanged at 76 per cent.

questions.stem: According to the note, what most likely explains the fall in claims?

options.text: Drivers claimed less often because the punctuality rate improved
options.misconception: invents a punctuality change the note rules out

options.text: The claim form became shorter, so fewer drivers bothered to use it
options.misconception: attributes the fall to convenience rather than friction

options.text: Claiming became harder, which suppressed claims without changing service
Fewer journeys qualified once the working timetable changed
options.misconception: assumes a timetable change the note does not record

questions.explanation: Punctuality was unchanged, so service did not improve; the fall followed a change to the claim form, which made claiming harder. The other options invent changes the note does not record.
questions.hint: Check what the note says stayed constant.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Choose the use of concentrated reporting that directs resources to risk
questions.stem: A regulator wants to use concentrated reporting to find safety risks. Which approach makes best use of the data?

options.text: Rank staff by the number of reports they have made so the most diligent are recognised
options.misconception: rewards reporting volume rather than directing resources to risk

options.text: Group reports by location, equipment and time of day to find the common factor
Investigate the staff who make most reports to check the quality of their accounts
options.misconception: treats the reporters rather than the reported hazard as the subject

options.text: Reduce the volume of reporting by setting a higher threshold for what counts as a concern
options.misconception: discards the evidence instead of using it

questions.explanation: Concentration points to a shared condition, so grouping by location, equipment and time reveals the factor that can be fixed. Ranking or investigating reporters shifts attention from that hazard.
questions.hint: Ask what the reports have in common.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the accountability position created by an off-budget fund
questions.stem: A depot's manager holds a fund for crew welfare that receives a departmental grant and is spent without appearing in the published budget. Which statement best describes the accountability position?

options.text: Public money is being spent outside the figures the legislature approved
The manager has accepted responsibility for the fund, so the position is sound
options.misconception: treats personal accountability as a substitute for budgetary control

options.text: The fund is small enough that including it would only clutter the budget
options.misconception: judges significance by size rather than by principle

options.text: The grant makes the fund visible to the finance office, so it is not off-budget
options.misconception: mistakes finance-office visibility for budgetary inclusion

questions.explanation: Public money is spent outside the approved figures, so the budget no longer states the department's real commitments. Personal responsibility and finance-office visibility do not make spending voted.
questions.hint: Ask whether the spending was voted.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate declared net worth from assets and two liabilities
questions.stem: A dispatcher declares a house worth 210,000 pounds and a vehicle worth 12,000 pounds, against a mortgage of 135,000 pounds and a loan of 9,000 pounds. What is the declared net worth?

options.text: 222,000 pounds, which is the total value of the assets before liabilities
options.misconception: omits liabilities when computing net worth

options.text: 78,000 pounds, subtracting both liabilities from both assets
87,000 pounds, which counts the vehicle but not the car loan
options.misconception: ignores one of the declared liabilities

options.text: 69,000 pounds, which subtracts the car loan twice
options.misconception: subtracts the same liability twice

questions.explanation: Assets of 210,000 plus 12,000 give 222,000 pounds, and liabilities of 135,000 plus 9,000 give 144,000, leaving a net worth of 78,000 pounds. The distractors either omit liabilities, omit one of them or count one twice.
questions.hint: Add each side, then subtract.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Read the scope of an audit office from the work it performs
questions.stem: An audit office reviewed 45 depot expense claims, examined the fuel reconciliation at 12 depots, and followed up eight findings raised three years earlier. What does this pattern of work show?

options.text: The office has a mandate restricted to financial transactions only
options.misconception: treats broad scope as narrow scope

options.text: The office has become the operational controller of the depot network
options.misconception: mistakes coverage of operations for control of operations

options.text: The office has focused on compliance because complaints have declined
options.misconception: invents a cause for the pattern of work

options.text: The office's mandate covers money, operational records and the follow-up of its own findings

questions.explanation: Reviewing claims, examining fuel reconciliations and revisiting earlier findings together show a mandate reaching expenditure, operational records and the audit's own output. None of that amounts to operational control, and no cause for the pattern is given.
questions.hint: Add up the three kinds of work described.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Set out what a board should require before closing a long-standing finding
questions.stem: An audit finding has been carried forward for four consecutive years without closure. Explain what a board should require before it closes the finding.

answer.exemplar: A finding that has survived four annual cycles is no longer a project but a fact about the organisation, and closing it on the strength of another assurance that the control has been introduced would be recording the same answer for a fifth time. The board should require evidence of operation rather than evidence of intention: a sample of the underlying records, examined by someone other than the manager who owns the process, showing that the control was applied on the dates it should have been. If the control cannot be shown to work, the finding should stay open with the reason recorded, and the board should then consider whether the difficulty lies in the design of the control, in the level of resource given to it, or in the behaviour of the people operating it, because each of those calls for a different remedy. Where the risk has been consciously accepted, that acceptance should be recorded by a named senior officer with a review date, rather than inferred from the finding having been left in the report. Closure should also be visible: a published list of findings closed, with the evidence relied on, allows a reader to judge the standard being applied.

questions.explanation: A strong answer should require tested evidence of operation rather than renewed assurance, and ask whether the problem is design, resourcing or behaviour, with closure recorded and published rather than inferred from silence.
questions.hint: Ask what evidence of operation looks like.
